title: ACCC warns Black Friday shoppers to check AI answers and limit AI agents
excerpt: The ACCC says AI shopping tools can get things wrong and urges shoppers to verify answers and cap what AI agents can spend during the sales.
content_html:
The consumer watchdog has urged Australians to double-check what artificial intelligence tools tell them, and to limit what AI agents can do on their behalf, as shoppers head into the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales.

What happened

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission issued the warning on Friday, 27 November. It singled out a new wave of AI personal assistants now available in Australia, including Meta's Muse, OpenAI's ChatGPT dots and Google Tasks.

These agents can connect to a person's email, cloud storage and bank accounts, and some can now buy things for the user rather than just suggest them. The ACCC said that convenience comes with risks.

ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said many people liked being able to compare options quickly with AI, but added: "AI results can be wrong."

The regulator said AI tools can give confident answers that turn out to be false, can give different answers at different times, can be manipulated and can carry biases from the data they were trained on. It also warned that an AI agent may fail to recognise a scam and could present a fake product next to genuine ones.

Why it matters

The warning lands on one of the busiest shopping weekends of the year. The Australian Retailers Association and Roy Morgan have forecast record spending of $6.8 billion over the sales weekend, up 4 per cent on last year, Yahoo Finance reported.

Scammers are also using AI. The ACCC pointed to cloned online stores built with AI, deepfake advertisements that misuse brands or celebrities, and AI-generated product photos and descriptions that make goods look better than they are.

The regulator said it will continue its crackdown on misleading promotions, including a sweep of retail sectors over Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

What it means for you

The ACCC set out five tips for shoppers:

  • Verify important answers. Check with a reliable source, particularly for big purchases or anything involving health, money, safety or legal rights. For a major buy, go straight to the seller's own website.
  • Look for gaps. If an AI tool says a product or price is the best, confirm it with your own independent search.
  • Guard your personal details. Think carefully before giving an AI tool financial, medical or identity information.
  • Control what the agent can do. Review its permissions, decide the points at which it must ask for your approval, cap how much it can spend, and check any payment before it goes through.
  • Ask for a human. If a chatbot cannot fix a complaint, request help from a person, and keep screenshots or records of key conversations.

Using AI does not reduce your legal protections. Cass-Gottlieb said "their consumer guarantee rights under Australian Consumer Law do not change" when a purchase involves AI.

For small businesses, the message is that responsibility stays with the seller. The ACCC said businesses are accountable for what their chatbots and AI agents do, and are liable for misleading information whether it comes from staff, written material or an AI tool.

The regulator said businesses using AI should keep human oversight, test the tools' answers against competition and consumer law, and have a plan to catch and correct errors, identify affected customers and offer remedies. They should also give customers a clear route to a human when the AI cannot resolve a problem, and must not overstate what their AI agents can do.

What's next

The ACCC said it will publish an update to its 2025 snapshot of the AI industry in the coming months, focused on AI agents and so-called agentic commerce, where software makes purchases for consumers.

Its retail sweep will run through the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period.
